item.title: Connecting the dots: How rising government bond yields could hurt your retirement savings
item.description:
Just imagine you have a decent sum of money and that you are looking for good investment to get into. Now, someone comes up to you and offers you a relatively safe investment that pays 5% a year. That doesn't sound too shabby, no? Especially when you don't have to pick your brain in trying to find the next big stock market winner.

Well, that's essentially what government bonds are offering in this market. With Treasury yields hovering around 5% lately, that proposition is looking rather attractive.

So, what happens when investors can earn decent returns without taking much risk? All of a sudden, everything else has to work a little harder to compete with what those bonds are offering.

I mean, think about it. If you can earn 5% from a US government bond, would you really want to take on the additional risk of investing in stocks for a similar return? Probably not. To compensate you for wanting to take on that risk, you'd want something extra in return. And that is where the trouble begins for stock markets.

When government bond yields rise, investors generally demand higher potential returns from riskier investments too. That can also mean paying less for company shares today, even if the businesses themselves haven't changed much.

Besides that, there's another problem to consider. Let's not forget that companies borrow money too. And when government borrowing costs rise, corporate borrowing rates often follow.

Let's take an example where a company wants to borrow $1 million to build a new factory. At 4% interest, that's $40,000 annually. At 7%, it's $70,000. That's an extra $30,000 every year that could otherwise have gone towards hiring workers, expanding the business, or even rewarding shareholders.

Now, imagine that very same thing happening across hundreds or even thousands of companies. Slower investment leads to weaker profits and that in turn puts pressure on stock valuations. That is not quite something that sounds good for your retirement portfolio, does it?

And here's the part I think people sometimes overlook. You don't have to own government bonds directly to feel the impact of all that. Your pension fund, retirement account, or long-term investment portfolio would almost certainly have a mix of both stocks and bonds.

So, rising yields can push down the market value of existing fixed-rate bonds while also weighing on share prices at the same time. Thus, that can leave retirement savings facing pressure from both sides of the equation.

Now, higher yields aren't exactly all bad. There is the fact that new bond investments can offer better income, which may benefit long-term savers. But for someone who might be approaching retirement, the timing of a market downturn can be especially painful.

As much as we might not think about it, the very fact of life investing is that a government borrowing more expensively today could very well end up affecting how comfortably you retire tomorrow.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin rallies on US-Iran deal hopes amid increasingly positive reports. What's next?
item.description:
Bitcoin remains mostly rangebound amid uncertainty around US-Iran negotiations and growing concerns about the macroeconomic outlook. We got an upward spike yesterday after Al-Arabiya reported that Qatar and Pakistan presented a compromise proposal that could pave the way for an agreement, but the momentum faded after a diplomat involved in the talks subsequently pushed back against reports that a deal was close.

Markets retain some hope of a breakthrough given the recent increase in positive headlines and the proximity to the US midterm elections. A deal would ease inflation and rate hike concerns and improve the risk sentiment, providing some short-term support for Bitcoin.

Another potential catalyst could be Friday's US Flash PMIs. A stronger than expected report could trigger a short-term relief rally on improved risk sentiment. However, it wouldn't change the bigger picture, as stronger economic data and persistent inflationary pressures would reinforce the need for further Fed rate hikes. A weak report, on the other hand, could intensify growth concerns and lead to risk aversion, putting further pressure on the cryptocurrency.

item.title: European markets steady for now but widening bond yield spreads offer a warning
item.description:
European equities are keeping steadier so far today with France's benchmark CAC 40 index even holding up by 0.3% on the session. Meanwhile, the euro is also only slightly lower against the dollar but is still holding above the 1.1200 level at around 1.1215 currently. That suggests traders are not quite rushing for the exits just yet.

That being said, I wouldn't be too quick to mistake the calmer mood for an improvement in the underlying risks for European markets. Not especially when the bond market is hinting at a different mood.

The France-Germany 10-year yield spread has widened further to around 158 bps today, marking its highest level since 2011. And if you look at the chart, we're now revisiting levels last seen during the height of the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis.

That's hardly a reassuring comparison, even if we are not quite talking about a repeat of those very same circumstances just yet.

In any case, the widening spread reflects the growing premium investors are demanding to hold French debt over German bonds. And with France's fiscal troubles and political uncertainty showing little signs of easing, there isn't much reason for bond investors to feel more comfortable at this stage.

So, what's next from here?

It will be important to watch out for any concerns about how this story could develop into something that is not just France anymore. And we might already be getting some early hints of that.

The Italy-Germany 10-year yield spread has also widened to nearly 119 bps today, threatening to retest the highs around 120-125 bps seen at the start of this month. If that spread continues to push higher alongside the France-Germany spread, it would suggest that investors are becoming more cautious about euro area sovereign debt more broadly. In other words, the story is starting to become more than just a French one.

That is where the risk of wider market contagion starts to creep into the picture. In turn, that could potentially weigh more heavily on European equities and the euro while complicating the ECB's policy outlook.

For now, the calm in broader markets is a welcome relief. However, I would be paying much closer attention to what is happening beneath the surface. With yield spreads at the risk of blowing up, there's every risk that this recovery in market sentiment could be a short-lived one.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Macro pulse: Is the BOJ about to raise interest rates at the worst possible time?
item.description:
I don't think anyone would want to the be in the BOJ's shoes right now. On the one hand, inflation pressures are giving policymakers every reason to keep raising interest rates. But on the other hand, Japan's economy is already dealing with expensive energy imports and a weak yen - not to mention a very uncertain global outlook.

If that isn't problematic enough, then here's the kicker. The inflation pressures that are building aren't exactly the kind that the BOJ has been hoping for.

The central bank has spent decades in trying to nurture a healthier cycle of rising wages, stronger consumer spending, and sustainable price increases. For the most part, those efforts went nowhere. And it took a global economic reset from the Covid pandemic to finally give Japan a get-out-of-jail-free card.

Remember, Japan spent much of the last thirty years struggling with stagnant wages and prices. Businesses were reluctant to raise prices, workers weren't getting any meaningful wage increases, and consumers had grown accustomed to things staying relatively cheap.

Then came the Covid pandemic, followed by global supply chain disruptions and a surge in commodity prices. Suddenly, businesses had little choice but to raise prices as inflation started making its way back into the Japanese economy. Initially, that was largely cost-push inflation too. But it also helped break Japan's long-standing reluctance to raise prices, while workers began pushing harder for higher wages to keep up with living costs.

And for a while, it looked like Japan was finally getting the sort of inflation that policymakers had spent years trying to achieve. But amid the US-Iran conflict this year, much of the latest surge in price pressures is coming from the other direction.

Higher oil prices and import costs are forcing businesses to pay more, with those increases eventually being passed on to consumers. Once again, it's another story of cost-push inflation. And unlike wage-driven inflation, it doesn't necessarily leave households with more money to spend. In fact, it is quite the opposite actually.

And Japan's latest trade figures underline the problem. The country recorded a ¥2.8 trillion trade deficit for the April to September period, more than double the roughly ¥1.2 trillion deficit recorded a year earlier. That is largely driven by a 20.4% surge in imports as soaring energy import costs take their toll.

This is where things get particularly awkward for the BOJ. The central bank has spent years trying to get inflation going but now it has to worry about whether the latest bout of price pressures might actually undermine the wage-driven recovery it has worked so hard to achieve.

So, where does that leave interest rates?

For now, markets are virtually ruling out a rate hike in October but are pricing in roughly a 74% probability of another move in December. That fits with the sort of messaging we have seen from the BOJ as of late, with the tightening pace still sticking around once every quarter in order to manage the risks of inflation overshooting.

Having said that, raising interest rates isn't going to make oil prices any cheaper. And while a stronger yen could provide some relief, that's hardly a given when Treasury yields remain elevated and the dollar continues to attract demand from traders across the globe.

All the while, higher borrowing costs could end up squeezing domestic spending and business investment at a time when Japan can ill afford another drag on growth.

Damned if you do, damned if you don't.

It's kind of ironic. The BOJ spent decades trying to escape an economy where prices wouldn't rise. But now, it risks tightening policy because prices appear to be rising for all the wrong reasons.

I'm not saying that another rate hike would necessarily be a mistake. However, I would argue that the margin for error is getting smaller. And for a central bank that has spent so long trying to get inflation right, the last thing it needs is to get the timing wrong.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Silver whipsaws on conflicting US-Iran deal reports as markets hope for breakthrough ahead of midterms
item.description:

The new proposal also included partial response to Iran's frozen funds demand.

The market cheered initially as expectations of an imminent deal grew stronger but then reversed after a diplomat involved in US-Iran talks said that negotiations continue and that reports of a deal being close were wrong.

Nevertheless, the markets retain some hope given the sudden increase of positive reports and the proximity to the midterm elections. Trump might want to secure at least a short-term deal to bring energy prices and Treasury yields lower, while boosting the stock market.

Another potential catalyst could be the US Flash PMIs data on Friday. item.title: HOLA PRIME SIMPLIFIES PROP TRADING RULES WITH LAUNCH OF IT’S RULEBOOK
item.description:
Hola Prime, a global proprietary trading firm, today announced the launch of TheRulebook, a consolidated rulebook designed to make trading rules and account conditions easier to access, understand and track.

The updated rulebook brings key information covering challenge passing criteria, conditions, trading rules, breach conditions and account requirements into one place. It also maintains transparent change logs, allowing traders to follow updates to the rules and understand how the firm's requirements evolve over time.

By centralising this information, Hola Prime aims to give traders a clearer reference point throughout their trading journey, from understanding account conditions before trading to reviewing the rules that apply to their accounts.

All Rules in One Place, With Transparent Change Logs

Prop trading rules and account conditions play an important role in how traders manage their accounts. Having access to the applicable requirements in one place helps traders understand their obligations without having to navigate multiple resources.

The Rulebook brings these requirements together in a single document, giving traders one central reference for the rules governing their accounts. The rulebook is designed to make access to information more straightforward and give traders greater clarity on the requirements they are expected to follow.

Three Restrictions Removed

As part of the update, Hola Prime has removed three restrictions that previously applied to funded accounts:

  • The 60% maximum concentration per trade
  • The 70% maximum margin rule
  • The three-minute Stop Loss deadline

These changes form part of Hola Prime's broader effort to simplify its trading conditions while making the applicable rules easier for traders to review.

A Clearer Process for Breach Appeals

While The Rulebook provides a central reference for trading rules and account conditions, Hola Prime also offers traders a way to challenge a breach they believe has been applied incorrectly.

Traders who have grounds to dispute a breach can submit an appeal through the available appeal process. Hola Prime's Risk Team reviews the circumstances and provides a written explanation of the outcome, whether the original breach is upheld or reversed.

This process gives traders a formal channel to raise concerns and seek clarification when they believe an account decision does not align with the applicable rules.

Making Rule Transparency Part of the Trader Experience

Somesh Kapuria, CEO of Hola Prime, said:

“Clear rules are an important part of a fair trading environment. Traders should be able to find the conditions that apply to their accounts without having to search across multiple resources. With The Rulebook, we are bringing those requirements together and maintaining transparent change logs so traders can keep track of updates. We have also removed three restrictions from Sim. funded accounts as part of our ongoing effort to make our trading conditions clearer and more straightforward.”

The Rulebook is available to Hola Prime traders on the official Hola Prime website.

About Hola Prime

Hola Prime is a global proprietary trading firm offering funded trading accounts to traders worldwide. The firm provides access to trading opportunities across major financial instruments, including forex, commodities and indices, with programs designed for different trading approaches.

Known for its 1-Hour Payout model, Hola Prime has received industry recognition, including the Global Most Transparent Prop Firm 2025 award by Finance Magnates and the Fastest Payout Prop Firm MEA 2026 award by UF Awards.

 

This article was written by IL Contributors at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why Treasury yields move together but become more volatile further out the curve
item.description:
Treasury yields are primarily driven by expectations for the future path of Federal Reserve monetary policy. This relationship is especially strong at the front end of the yield curve, where yields are closely linked to expectations about how the Fed will adjust interest rates over the near-term. However, monetary policy expectations remain important even at the long end of the curve. The difference is that longer-term yields are also more sensitive to changes in the economic outlook, inflation expectations and the compensation investors demand for holding long-duration bonds, called term premium.

The front-end is driven by monetary policy expectations

The 2-year Treasury yield is one of the most useful indicators of market expectations for Federal Reserve policy. If markets begin to expect the Fed to raise interest rates in the coming months, the two-year yield will generally rise. Conversely, if economic data weakens or inflation moderates, markets will start to price in rate cuts and the 2-year yield will generally fall.

The key point is that markets are forward-looking. Treasury yields reflect expectations for future short-term interest rates over the life of the bond. Consequently, yields will move well before the Fed actually changes its policy rate. That doesn't mean the market will always be right. Sometimes the market gets things wrong, but the change in expectations still drives yields higher or lower depending on the economic context and incoming information.

The long-end is still driven by monetary policy expectations

The 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields are often framed as though they move independently of the Fed. But that's misleading. Expectations for monetary policy remain a fundamental driver of longer-term yields, but their influence is more complex because investors must consider a much longer economic horizon.

A longer-term Treasury yield can be decomposed into two components: expected future short-term interest rates and a term premium. The first component links long-term yields directly to monetary policy expectations. If investors expect the Fed to maintain restrictive policy for longer, or believe that short-term rates will settle at a higher level over the coming decade, longer-term yields will generally face upward pressure.

The second component helps explain why long-term yields can move significantly even when expectations for the federal funds rate change very little. The term premium can rise when uncertainty about inflation increases for example, as investors will demand greater compensation for bearing duration risk. Changes in the supply and demand for Treasuries can also influence this premium, although it's a very minor part. The term premium is not seomthing that is observable or can be accurately calculated. It changes based on the economic context. 

Chart: Federal Funds Rate (black), 2y yield (red), 5y yield (green), 10y yield (violet), 30y yield (blue)

Long-term yields are more sensitive to growth and inflation

Although monetary policy expectations matter across the entire yield curve, the further we move out in maturity, the more economic developments can influence the outlook for interest rates over the longer run.

Suppose we get a very strong US PMI report that changes expectations about growth. The data might lead markets to expect more Fed rate hikes, pushing the 2-year yield higher, but the implications for the 10-year yield can extend beyond the next few Fed meetings. Stronger growth could imply a higher equilibrium real interest rate, stronger underlying demand and potentially greater inflationary pressure. If investors think that the economy can sustain higher interest rates over the long run, long-term yields may rise by more than the 2-year yield.

This is what generally leads to a bear steepening of the curve as long-term bonds fall faster than short-term bonds. That's exactly what happened after the September's US Flash PMI, as you can see in the chart below.

The same logic applies to inflation. A temporary increase in inflation might change expectations for the next few Fed meetings, but a persistent inflation shock can alter expectations for inflation over many years. Investors may also demand a higher term premium because of increased uncertainty.

The reverse is also true. A deterioration in the growth outlook can push yields lower as markets anticipate monetary easing. This is why before an economic slowdown or even a recession, the 10-year yield falls faster than the 2-year yield. This can happen even during a Federal Reserve tightening cycle if the markets think that the central bank overtightened and will have to cut interest rates sooner than expected.

This is why longer-term yields can experience larger swings than shorter-term yields. They reflect not only the expected response of monetary policy in the near-term but also changing views about the economy over a longer horizon.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stock market open: Stocks tread cautiously as French bond market keeps the mood in check
item.description:
European equities are keeping to a rather subdued start on Wednesday, with major indices showing little appetite to build on the recovery in Wall Street overnight. The opening changes:

  • Eurostoxx +0.1%
  • Germany DAX -0.1%
  • France CAC 40 +0.1%
  • UK FTSE -0.2%
  • Spain IBEX -0.3%
  • Italy FTSE MIB -0.1%

There's not much to get excited about from the early moves but I would argue that the bigger story in Europe right now isn't what we're seeing in the equities space. It's what is happening in the bond market.

The France-Germany 10-year yield spread has widened to around 154 bps today, pushing above the 150 bps mark and keeping near its widest levels since the Eurozone debt crisis in 2012.

After a relentless climb since September, the spread is now pushing past the 150 bps resistance area that had capped several attempts to move higher earlier this month. In simpler terms, what the chart tells us is that investors are demanding a much bigger premium to hold French government debt over German bonds. And with France's fiscal troubles and political uncertainty showing little sign of easing, it's difficult to see what might turn that sentiment around anytime soon.

The major worry right now isn't just about higher borrowing costs. It's also about confidence in Europe's second-largest economy and how persistent pressure in French bonds might eventually weigh more heavily on the euro and broader regional assets.

And mind you, we don't need a full-blown debt crisis for that to happen either.

As such, I wouldn't be comfortable in reading too much into the lack of selling pressures at the open. Stocks may be holding steadier and keeping somewhat cautious, but the bond market is already starting to act up.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Gold price eyes $4,100 support as $4,200 resistance keeps bulls in check
item.description:
Gold continues to find itself on the defensive in the past few weeks, as the precious metal is unable to gather much reprieve from both a fundamental and technical perspective.

On the former, the bond market continues to play a key role. With 10-year Treasury yields hovering above 5%, the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset like gold is rather difficult to ignore. And that angle currently outweighs the fact that gold has historically been a solid hedge against geopolitical and inflation risks.

Meanwhile, the technicals are also reflecting that struggle quite clearly. Looking at the 4-hour chart, sellers have repeatedly defended the $4,200-20 region since the start of October. The 100-period moving average (red line) has also consistently capped recovery attempts, with the latest rejection leaving gold hovering around $4,114 today.

The daily chart also tells a similar story with gold price action continue to hold below the key daily moving averages, keeping sellers in control:

The $4,200-20 region is the immediate hurdle to any upside push, while the $4,100-17 area is now the key support zone to watch.

In other words, we are seeing a consolidation phase for gold price and one that has clear technical levels defining it. That leaves us with two possible scenarios.

For the bulls, defending the $4,100-17 region is the first priority. But in looking to the upside, they need to muster a convincing break above $4,200-20 first. Only then can the bulls start taking aim at the 100-day moving average at around $4,232 currently before looking to $4,300 next. As for catalysts, easing Treasury yields would certainly help alongside continued central bank demand for the precious metal in the bigger picture.

For the bears, a firm break below $4,100 would expose the $4,000 psychological mark and potentially the July low near $3,960 as the next targets. As for catalysts, the very fact that 10-year Treasury yields continue to keep above 5% is a strong reason to keep broader markets on edge and put gold in a tight spot.

But for now though, the predicament is relatively straightforward. Gold price remains caught between $4,100-17 and $4,200-20 with there being neither enough conviction from safety hedge to offset the pressure from higher borrowing costs; vice versa.

So until something gives way, it's a bit of a waiting game. Buyers have the $4,100-17 region to defend, while sellers are keeping a firm grip on the $4,200-20 area. But with Treasury yields still elevated, I would argue that the burden remains on gold bulls to prove they can turn things around.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: UK September CPI inflation rises to 3.5%, reinforces BOE November rate hike expectations
item.description:
• UK September CPI +3.5% vs +3.4% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.1%
  • UK September core CPI +2.8% vs +2.8% y/y expected
  • Prior +2.6%

As expected, headline annual inflation surged in the Uk during the past month with the reading being the highest since October last year.

Higher energy costs are the main culprit here as transport, particularly motor fuels, made the largest upward contribution to the change in annual price pressures. Of note, the average price of petrol rose by 8.2 pence per litre between August and September 2026, compared with a fall of 0.2 pence per litre between August and September 2025. The average price stood at 169.5 pence per litre in September 2026. This is the highest price recorded since August 2022.

Besides the rise in headline prices, core prices also showed an uptick with the annual estimate climbing to 2.8%. This is one spot that will pressure the BOE to tighten policy further, reinforcing market expectations of a move in November next. Looking at the details, services inflation continues to run up to 3.7% in September from 3.4% previously.

As such, that is a hint that price pressures are broadening and if not, it just reaffirms the notion that services inflation is still extremely sticky and stubborn. But whatever the case, it just means the BOE cannot rest on their laurels in trying to battle against the inflation monster.

Traders had already priced in roughly 96% odds of a 25 bps rate hike for November, so the report here will do little to change that as the numbers only help to reinforce the market view. GBP/USD is still trading little changed at 1.3365 on the day currently.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Social unrest pressures European markets
item.description:
Protests that began in France a few weeks ago over poor school conditions have escalated into clashes with police, looting, and arson amid rising fuel prices and the cost of living. 

The problem is that France’s budget deficit reached 5.1% of GDP in 2025, while public debt approached 120%, leaving the government with little room to support households. 

Actually, it is now pushing for €54 billion in spending cuts in its 2027 budget, as the fiscal outlook could otherwise deteriorate further, but getting them through amid social unrest won’t be easy. 

Demonstrations also took place in Liège, Belgium, in early October before spreading to other cities across Wallonia and Brussels, as well as Ireland, Spain, Italy, Germany, Greece, and Austria.

While largely peaceful, the unrest is putting pressure on European bond markets and the EUR/USD currency pair.

In France, for example, long-term government bond yields have reached 5.5%, surpassing US yields for the first time since 2013. The cost of insuring against a French default has also climbed to its highest level since 2013.

European equities are also under pressure, with rising energy prices amid the war in the Middle East, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, and concerns over returns on AI investments adding to the strain and further weighing on sentiment. 

 

What could calm the markets?

 

A strong earnings season.

And the good news is that consensus estimates point to 20.7% earnings growth for the STOXX Europe 600, driven by energy, technology, and industrials. Higher gas and oil prices are boosting energy profits, while the AI investment boom is driving demand for European equipment and industrial solutions.

According to Reuters, tech earnings could rise by nearly 33%, while industrial profits could grow by 11%. Banks could provide an additional boost.

Of course, much will depend on companies’ outlooks for Q4 and 2027, how well they protect margins, and whether they can turn revenue growth into cash flow. 

It is also worth considering that earnings estimates have also been revised up for Q3, so beating expectations may be harder.

But even if they do, the relief may be short-lived, as Europe’s underlying fiscal problems remain unresolved. Inflation risks are also still there, meaning central banks may have to stay hawkish, which is hardly good news for the economy or financial markets. 

This article was written by IL Contributors at investinglive.com.

item.title: GBP/EUR Surge: Can the Rally Continue?
item.description:
Sterling has strengthened against the euro as expectations of higher UK interest rates collide with growing uncertainty across European financial markets. On October 20, the pound reached its strongest level against the single currency since May 2025, with the exchange rate trading around 83.95 pence per euro (after a low at around 83.89). The currency was mostly supported by UK labour-market data that reinforced expectations of a Bank of England (BoE) rate increase on November 5.

EUR/GBP Daily Chart - Source: TradingView

However, the pound's advance is not simply a reflection of improving UK economic fundamentals. Political unrest in France, rising European sovereign borrowing costs and surging energy prices are also shaping currency markets. With money markets almost fully pricing in a 25-basis-point BoE rate hike, the key question is whether sterling can extend its gains or whether expectations have already gone too far.

BoE Rate-Hike Expectations Support Sterling, but the Labour Market Sends Mixed Signals

The latest UK employment figures have strengthened the case for monetary tightening, although they do not provide an unequivocal signal that the economy can withstand a prolonged cycle of rate increases.

Annual growth in regular wages reached 3.7% in the three months to August, exceeding economists' expectations of 3.6%. The unemployment rate also edged down to 4.7%, its lowest level since mid-2025, while preliminary payroll estimates suggested that employment conditions may be stabilising. These developments followed a run of stronger-than-expected UK economic data.

Employment Rate and Wage Growth in the UK - Source: Reuters

For the BoE, the combination matters because persistent wage growth can contribute to domestic inflation, particularly if labour costs remain elevated. If policymakers believe that inflation will stay above their 2% target for longer than expected, tighter monetary policy may be necessary.

Markets have responded accordingly. Money-market futures were almost fully pricing in a 25-basis-point increase at the November 5 meeting, which would lift the Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%. Investors were also anticipating further increases into 2027, although expectations for a sustained tightening cycle remain less certain. 

Higher expected UK interest rates can support sterling by improving the relative return available on pound-denominated assets. However, the latest employment report contains an important counterpoint.

The number of vacancies fell to 691,000 in the July-to-September period, its lowest level outside the pandemic era since 2014. The decline suggests that businesses, particularly smaller firms facing higher employment costs, remain reluctant to recruit. The Office for National Statistics also reported that payroll employment remained weaker than a year earlier. 

This creates a gap between market expectations and the underlying economic picture. Wage growth and falling unemployment strengthen the argument for a November rate increase, but declining vacancies point to fragile labour demand.

The data therefore provide a stronger case for a possible near-term hike than for assuming that several additional increases will necessarily follow. If the BoE raises rates as expected but signals caution about subsequent decisions, some of sterling's monetary-policy support could fade.

European Political Turmoil Adds to the Euro's Vulnerability

Sterling is also benefiting from pressure on the euro, as investors reassess the political and fiscal outlook across Europe.

France has become a particular source of concern. Renewed demonstrations and unrest have added to uncertainty surrounding the government's ability to pass its 2027 budget and address the country's sizeable deficit. At the same time, French government bond yields have approached levels last seen in 2002, while the spread between French and German 10-year yields has widened significantly. 

These developments matter for the single currency because persistent sovereign bond-market stress can undermine confidence in the eurozone's economic and financial stability. If investors begin to demand higher risk premiums across several member states, concerns about financial fragmentation could intensify. Of course, France's difficulties should not be treated as an automatic signal of a wider eurozone crisis. The implications for the single currency will depend on whether political and fiscal pressures remain concentrated in France or spread to other European markets.

For the GBP/EUR, the distinction is important. Sterling can appreciate because investors become more confident in the UK outlook, because they become less confident in the eurozone, or through a combination of both.

The Oil Shock Could Complicate the BoE's Next Move

The Middle East conflict introduces another variable that could reshape the outlook for sterling and the euro: energy prices.

Brent crude climbed above $111 per barrel on October 20, reaching its highest level since May, amid persistent disruption risks around the Strait of Hormuz and limited progress towards ending the conflict. The prospect of further interruptions to energy shipments has kept markets concerned about supply and inflation.

Daily UK Oil Chart - Source: ActivTrades

For the UK, higher oil and gas prices could push inflation higher through transport, household energy bills and business costs. If these pressures persist, the BoE may face greater difficulty bringing inflation back towards its 2% target, strengthening the argument for higher interest rates.

That could initially support sterling, particularly if investors expect the BoE to tighten policy more aggressively than the European Central Bank (ECB). Yet the relationship between energy prices, interest rates and currencies is not straightforward.

Higher energy costs also reduce households' disposable income, squeeze corporate margins and potentially weaken economic growth. If the shock becomes sufficiently severe, markets could begin to question whether further monetary tightening would damage the UK economy rather than simply contain inflation.

The BoE has already warned that prolonged energy-price volatility could make inflation more persistent and increase the likelihood of further tightening. Its September decision left Bank Rate at 3.75%, while acknowledging the risks arising from the conflict.  The ECB faces a similar dilemma, although the consequences differ according to each economy's exposure to energy imports, inflation dynamics and fiscal position.

The key risk for sterling is therefore that the energy shock initially supports rate-hike expectations but eventually undermines the growth outlook. If markets begin to focus more heavily on the economic damage, the pound could lose some of its current advantage.

Can GBP/EUR Extend Its Rally?

The outlook for the GBP/EUR will depend on whether the BoE delivers the expected rate increase and how policymakers assess the risks beyond November. Three scenarios stand out.

Sterling could extend its gains if UK inflation remains persistent, the BoE raises rates and French political uncertainty continues to weigh on the euro. A further widening in expected UK-eurozone interest-rate differentials could provide additional support, although much will depend on how much tightening is already reflected in market prices.

The currency pair could consolidate if the November hike is delivered but the BoE signals that subsequent decisions will depend on incoming data. With vacancies falling and hiring demand remaining weak, policymakers may be reluctant to validate expectations of a prolonged series of increases. If European market tensions also ease, sterling's relative advantage could diminish.

The euro could recover if energy prices retreat, political risks in Europe subside or markets reassess the expected pace of UK monetary tightening. A deterioration in British growth prospects could also undermine sterling, particularly if higher energy costs squeeze household spending and corporate profitability.

For traders, the distinction between the expected November decision and the outlook for rates in 2027 is important. A widely anticipated rate increase may provide limited additional support if it is already priced into the GBP/EUR evolution. Future price movements could depend more on the BoE's guidance, inflation data and developments in the Middle East.

Sources: Reuters, The Wall Street Journal, ONS, Bank of England, Yahoo Finance

item.title: FX option expiries for 21 October 10am New York cut
item.description:
There are a couple of key expiry levels to take note of on the day, as highlighted in bold below.

The first ones are for EUR/USD with the expiries layered at the 1.1195 to 1.1200 region. The strikes are holding within 30 pips of the spot price and together, they are quite chunky in size. As such, the combined €4.3 billion in expiries could exert some pull towards the 1.1200 region heading into the cut. Or if anything else, they might also help reinforce the area as an intraday focal point.

Having said that, broader euro and dollar sentiment will still take precedence alongside what else is happening with the bond market of course.

The euro has its own set of problems with the France-Germany 10-year yield spread hitting 1.52% yesterday, its highest since 2012. That hasn't reverberated all too strongly yet but will continue to be a key risk factor for the single currency this week.

Meanwhile, dollar sentiment is still very much tied to what is happening in the bond market. And for now, Treasury yields are not up to much so that is affording broader markets a bit more of breather in the first half of the week at least.

Besides the expiries for EUR/USD, there is also one for USD/JPY at the 158.00 level - less than 10 pips away from the spot price. The expiry level here could keep price action more contained in acting as a bit of a magnet ahead of the cut. That is especially the case as USD/JPY price action shows that the pair has been weaving in and around the 158.00 level for more than two weeks already.

Any upside momentum in the pair remains more limited closer to the 200-day moving average at 158.57, so that will also be a key technical consideration for now.

But as a reminder, options-related flows can influence short-term price action rather than necessarily dictate direction. And that is especially the case when there are broader fundamental drivers are in play, such as what we're seeing in the current market landscape. Dollar sentiment, the overall risk mood, and the bond market are all key drivers that should likely have a bigger say on price action at the moment.

item.title: BOJ policymaker Himino warns of upside inflation risks as Japan nears 2% target
item.description:
• Underlying inflation is quite close to BOJ's 2% target
  • Expect underlying inflation to converge to levels consistent with BOJ's target
  • Medium, long-term inflation expectations continue to heighten
  • Financial conditions remain accommodative
  • Real interest rates remain low
  • Delay in adjusting policy could see inflation risks materialise, hurt the economy
  • Upside risks to prices are high

The remarks from BOJ deputy governor, Ryozo Himino, above are not anything that we haven't heard of from the central bank. It mainly juts reinforces the narrative that Japan is getting closer to achieving its long-sought inflation target and that the central bank now has to be careful about letting things run too hot.

The most striking part of his comments is arguably the warning about delaying policy adjustments. But even then, there's no explicit hint that they are going to push for another rate hike sooner rather than later. And that is well reflected in the market pricing as well.

As things stand, traders are virtually ruling out a move at the October meeting but are pricing in roughly 74% odds of another rate hike in December. That is a rather telling contrast, especially when you consider Himino's warning that delaying policy adjustments could allow inflation risks to materialise and ultimately hurt the economy.

That doesn't mean that policymakers are not serious about their remarks. I would say that in Himino's case, his remarks aren't necessarily a push for an October move. Rather, they reinforce the argument that the BOJ cannot afford to sit on its hands for too long. But that's about it. They are neither an explicit confirmation about a move in December as well.

In any case, the takeaway for the yen is that further BOJ tightening remains firmly on the agenda. October may be a foregone conclusion for markets, but December is a different story.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Heads up: UK September CPI inflation report due today, BOE rate hike for November almost fully priced in
item.description:
The UK CPI report for September is the main highlight on the economic calendar today, with the release due at 0600 GMT. The inflation numbers will be heavily watched as it will have a lot to say about what comes next on the BOE outlook, even if traders are almost fully pricing in another 25 bps move in November.

Here's what to expect from the report:

  • Headline CPI: +3.4% y/y expected (Prior +3.1%)
  • Core CPI: +2.8% y/y expected (Prior +2.6%)

The estimates show that another pickup in inflation pressures is expected this time around. That's hardly good news for the BOE with price pressures already running well above its 2% target.

Higher energy costs are expected to remain a key driver, but I would argue that the more important thing to watch today will be the underlying inflation details. In particular, how stubborn services prices will be once again. Any signs of broader price pressures taking hold will only make the BOE's balancing act more difficult.

Looking at market pricing, traders are already pricing in roughly 96% odds of a 25 bps rate hike for 5 November next. As such, I reckon even a hotter inflation reading will do little to change expectations for the immediate decision. Instead, it could strengthen the case for further tightening beyond November. In that lieu, odds of a back-to-back move in December as well are seen at around 61% today. So, how that changes on a hotter-than-expected report will be the crucial point to be mindful of.

On the flip side, a softer-than-expected report could be the more interesting outcome. It might not be enough to derail a November move entirely, but it could see traders pare back some of their more aggressive BOE rate expectations.

Besides that, let's not forget that there is also the autumn budget on 28 October is just around the corner. That will also likely be another key consideration that the BOE has to take into account before their next meeting, aside from the inflation numbers today.

For a more detailed breakdown of the inflation outlook, BOE rate expectations, and budget implications, check out the full UK CPI preview here.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: RBA’s Hauser puts November hike in play
item.description:
• NEXTDC shares plunge 44% as power delays expose AI data centre bottleneck
  • Nvidia in talks to invest hundreds of millions in Firmus after AI cloud firm’s IPO flop
  • US intel says Putin ordered NATO sabotage drive, Leipzig drone attack an opening shot
  • Japan’s Katayama sees no gap with BOJ, says wage-driven inflation is near
  • PBOC sets USD/ CNY mid-point today at 6.7192 (vs. estimate at 6.6779)

  • Citadel’s Griffin says AI “almost certainly” a bubble, even as demand signals stay strong
  • SpaceX’s Musk says Tesla merger good idea but far from certain, needs 50% of Tesla shares
  • UBS flags 3 tests for the AI trade as Meta kicks off mega-cap tech earnings
  • Super Micro shares jump 14% as preliminary revenue tops forecast by about $4 billion
  • Goldman Sachs says 6% nominal growth, not 5% yields, is what matters for small caps
  • More from RBA’s (hawkish) Hauser: Q3 trimmed mean set to run hotter than expected
  • BOJ seen lifting rates to 1.50% in December as 69% of economists expect a Q4 hike
  • RBA’s Hauser says inflation outlook worse than forecast ahead of 3 November decision
  • JPMorgan sees Bitcoin returning 10% a year: why volatility makes that hard to collect
  • Anthropic IPO draft shows nearly 15-fold revenue jump and $600 billion in compute deals
  • Boeing wins FAA approval for 737 MAX 10, unlocking nearly 1,500 orders after 7-year wait
  • Oil: Private survey of inventory shows a huge headline crude oil draw, greater than expected
  • Swiss regulator FINMA approves first retail Bitcoin ETF, waives diversification rules

Summary:

  • RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook looks worse than forecast, the quarterly trimmed mean is likely to exceed expectations and capacity pressures are more elevated than assumed
  • Goldman Sachs now expects the RBA to raise the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on 3 November, having previously forecast no change
  • The Australian dollar rose on Hauser’s remarks but gave back the gains to be little changed on the session
  • NEXTDC shares plunged 44% after the data centre operator cut FY27 guidance on grid power delays
  • A Reuters poll found most economists expect the BOJ to raise rates to 1.50% in December; Japan’s September exports rose 16.7%, below forecast
  • South Korea’s KOSPI jumped more than 5%, triggering a buy-side sidecar; the Nikkei 225 rose 1.1%, the Shanghai Composite fell 0.4% and the Hang Seng slipped 0.3%
  • China’s youth unemployment rate eased to 18% in September from 18.9%
  • The FAA certified Boeing’s 737 MAX 10; SpaceX and Netflix reported results and Super Micro issued a surprise upgrade

Australia: Hauser signals fifth hike risk

Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser delivered the most significant news of the Asian session, signalling that a fifth rate rise this year is a live option at the Board’s next meeting on 3 November.

Speaking at a fireside chat at Citi’s Australia and New Zealand Investment Conference in Sydney, Hauser said the inflation outlook looks worse than the RBA had forecast and that the quarterly trimmed mean, the bank’s preferred measure of underlying inflation, appears set to come in higher than expected. He said capacity pressures in the economy are more elevated than anticipated and that firms are reporting cost pressures as their number one problem.

Hauser stressed that inflation has been high for a very long time and that the RBA cannot allow inflation expectations to drift away from target. He said the bank has to respond to supply shocks to keep expectations anchored, and that while policy cannot target current inflation, that does not mean current inflation is unimportant.

He acknowledged some offsets. September’s labour report was a little weaker than expected, and while unemployment remains quite low, the labour market is easing. Housing data has also slowed, and he said monetary policy is working. Hauser added that forecasts are still being finalised and he does not know for sure what the Board will decide.

Goldman Sachs subsequently changed its call and now expects the RBA to raise the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% in November, having previously forecast a hold. The cash rate stands at 4.60% after the 29 September hike, the fourth of 2026. September-quarter CPI data is due on 28 October, and the decision follows at 2.30pm Sydney time on 3 November (03:30 GMT, 22:30 ET on 2 November).

The Australian dollar rose on Hauser’s remarks but failed to follow through and was little changed on the session.

In equities, NEXTDC shares plunged 44% after the data centre operator cut its FY27 underlying EBITDA guidance to A$245 million to A$265 million, from A$385 million to A$410 million. Grid works for its Melbourne M3 site were suspended after community opposition, pushing additional power supply into FY28. The company froze new development projects.

Japan: December BOJ hike expected

A Reuters poll showed 69% of economists expect the Bank of Japan to raise its policy rate to 1.50% this quarter, with about 80% of those naming a month choosing December rather than the meeting ending 30 October. Most respondents warned that further dissent from government-nominated board members could weigh on the yen.

Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said Japan is on the cusp of sustained, wage-driven inflation and that she sees no gap between the government and the BOJ, after a lawmaker asked whether planned tax cuts could clash with rate hikes.

September exports rose 16.7% year on year, a 13th straight gain driven by AI and chip demand but below the 20.1% forecast. Imports rose 18.9% as delayed crude deliveries trimmed the energy bill, narrowing the trade deficit to ¥536.6 billion, wider than the ¥181 billion expected.

China and South Korea

China’s urban youth unemployment rate, covering 16 to 24-year-olds excluding students, eased to 18% in September from 18.9% in August, which had been the highest reading in 12 months, National Bureau of Statistics data showed.

South Korea’s KOSPI surged more than 5%, with KOSPI 200 futures up 5% triggering a buy-side sidecar that suspended programme trading for five minutes. It was the first such trigger in two months, driven by strong foreign net buying.

Markets

Asian equities were mixed. Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.1%, while the Shanghai Composite fell 0.4% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slipped 0.3%. Oil prices firmed slightly and gold was largely flat.

Corporate: earnings, Boeing and AI

The US Federal Aviation Administration granted final certification to Boeing’s 737 MAX 10, clearing the largest version of its best-selling jet for delivery after nearly seven years of delays and unlocking close to 1,500 orders.

SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of about $14.6 billion, well above forecasts, with its AI segment contributing more than half. On the earnings call, chief executive Elon Musk said a merger with Tesla would be a good idea but is far from certain, and that AI compute demand is likely to stay strong.

Netflix beat on third-quarter profit but guided fourth-quarter earnings below expectations and lowered its full-year free cash flow forecast to about $12 billion.

Super Micro Computer released a surprise preliminary update lifting September-quarter revenue to $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, far above prior guidance, sending its shares up 14% after hours.

Separately, Nvidia is in talks to invest in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus Grid after it scrapped its IPO, The Information reported, and Citadel founder Ken Griffin said AI is almost certainly in a bubble. Meta Platforms reports after the US close on Wednesday, opening mega-cap tech earnings. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NEXTDC shares plunge 44% as power delays expose AI data centre bottleneck
item.description:
NEXTDC’s downgrade is a stark example of a risk investors have tended to treat as theoretical: that grid access and local opposition, not customer demand, cap how fast data centre capacity can be built. The read-through extends well beyond Australia, as operators and AI cloud providers globally depend on utilities and planning authorities that move more slowly than hyperscaler spending plans. It echoes the warning in Anthropic’s draft IPO prospectus, reported this week, that resistance to data centres is becoming more organised across jurisdictions. Investors may now apply a larger discount to contracted-but-undelivered capacity across the sector, particularly where projects depend on new grid connections.

-

NEXTDC had the customers and the contracts, but not the electricity, and its 44% share collapse shows the AI build-out now runs only as fast as the local grid and the local council allow.

Summary:

  • NEXTDC shares fell 44% in early trading after the company cut its FY27 guidance
  • Underlying EBITDA guidance was lowered to A$245 million to A$265 million, from A$385 million to A$410 million; net revenue guidance cut to A$475 million to A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million
  • The downgrade stems from delays to grid works by Jemena Electricity Networks for the M3 Melbourne data centre, suspended in September after community opposition, safety concerns and a lack of council consent
  • Works are not expected to restart before February 2027, with extra grid supply now expected in FY28; the affected contracts were worth about A$140 million in prior guidance
  • All new development projects and land purchases are on hold, and FY27 capex guidance was cut to A$4.5 billion to A$5 billion
  • NEXTDC reported about A$8.7 billion of liquidity, including about A$1.3 billion in cash, and remains within its debt covenants

Access to electricity has emerged as a hard limit on the data centre build-out, after Australian operator NEXTDC slashed its earnings forecast because the power needed for a major Melbourne facility will arrive a year later than planned.

NEXTDC shares plunged 44% in early trading after the company cut its fiscal 2027 underlying EBITDA guidance to A$245 million to A$265 million, from A$385 million to A$410 million. Net revenue guidance was lowered to A$475 million to A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million.

The problem is not demand. The capacity at its M3 Melbourne site remains contracted to customers. Instead, grid works being carried out by Jemena Electricity Networks were suspended in September following community and stakeholder opposition, safety concerns and the absence of local council consent while further consultation takes place. Chief executive Craig Scroggie said Jemena did not expect the works to restart before February 2027, pushing the next increase in grid supply to M3 into fiscal 2028.

That delay defers the delivery and billing of contracted capacity that had contributed about A$140 million to both revenue and EBITDA in the previous forecast. The contracts include service-level credits for delays and, in some cases, termination rights.

Planning approval is also slipping. A Victorian government decision on later stages of the M3 development is now expected in 2027, with the state entering caretaker conventions on 3 November ahead of its 28 November election.

NEXTDC has put all new development projects and land acquisitions on hold, focusing spending on capacity due over the next 12 to 18 months, and its board will consider selling development sites not needed in the near term. Fiscal 2027 capex guidance was cut to A$4.5 billion to A$5 billion, from A$5.25 billion to A$5.75 billion. The company said it had about A$8.7 billion of liquidity at 30 September and remains within its financial covenants.

The episode highlights a risk that extends well beyond one company or one city. As AI drives record investment in computing capacity, the pace of delivery increasingly depends on utilities, planners and local communities. Anthropic’s draft IPO prospectus, reported this week, flagged growing and more coordinated political resistance to data centres as a business risk. NEXTDC’s downgrade suggests investors may need to price that risk into contracted capacity across the sector.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia in talks to invest hundreds of millions in Firmus after AI cloud firm’s IPO flop
item.description:
A fresh Nvidia investment would reassure holders of neocloud debt and equity that the sector’s largest supplier remains willing to support it, even as public markets turn more selective. The flip side is that Nvidia backing companies that buy its chips may sharpen questions about how much AI infrastructure demand depends on vendor financing rather than independent capital, an issue that sits at the heart of the bubble debate Ken Griffin revived on Tuesday. For Nvidia shares, the amounts involved are small, so the signal matters more than the money. The episode also suggests the IPO window for AI infrastructure firms is narrowing, pushing more of them toward private and strategic funding.

-

When public investors walked away from Firmus, Nvidia appears ready to step in, a reminder that the AI cloud boom still leans heavily on its biggest supplier.

Summary:

  • Nvidia is in talks to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Firmus Grid, according to The Information, as reported by Bloomberg (gated)
  • The talks follow Firmus’s decision earlier this month to scrap an IPO that would have been one of Australia’s largest
  • Firmus struggled to attract global investors, who have become more cautious on AI companies
  • Nvidia is already an investor in Firmus and several of its peers
  • The move signals continued Nvidia support for neoclouds, a group of heavily indebted AI cloud providers
  • Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment

Nvidia is in talks to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Firmus Grid, an AI cloud company that abandoned its initial public offering earlier this month, The Information reported, according to Bloomberg.

The discussions signal that Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, intends to keep supporting so-called neoclouds, according to the report, which cited people familiar with the talks. Neoclouds are specialist providers that rent out AI computing capacity, competing with the large cloud platforms run by the biggest tech groups. Many have taken on heavy debt to buy chips and build data centres, and the sector has come under pressure as investors grow more cautious.

Nvidia is already an investor in Firmus and in several of its peers. A spokesperson for the company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The talks follow Firmus’s decision to scrap a listing that would have ranked among Australia’s largest. The company struggled to draw global investors, who have become more wary of AI companies, Bloomberg reported. Bloomberg News had previously reported that Firmus was weighing other funding options.

The report adds to a mixed picture for AI infrastructure. On one side, demand signals remain strong: Super Micro Computer this week released a surprise update showing September-quarter revenue far ahead of its own guidance, and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk said compute remains so scarce that older Nvidia chips now rent for more than when new. On the other, public investors are showing more selectivity, and Citadel founder Ken Griffin said on Tuesday that AI is almost certainly in a bubble.

Nvidia’s willingness to back customers that buy its chips supports the neocloud model in the short term, but it also raises questions about how much of the sector’s growth relies on its main supplier. The size and terms of any Firmus investment, and whether other backers join, will indicate how much confidence remains in the neocloud business outside Nvidia itself.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US intel says Putin ordered NATO sabotage drive, Leipzig drone attack an opening shot
item.description:
The report raises the perceived risk of escalation between Russia and NATO, which would tend to support European defence stocks and weigh on European risk sentiment if officials respond with tougher measures. The energy channel is the one to watch: Russia’s diesel supply deal with Washington and the pause in new US sanctions were aimed partly at keeping Moscow out of the war with Iran, so any rupture in that arrangement could tighten fuel markets already strained by the Middle East conflict. Drone strikes on commercial ships in the Black Sea add a shipping risk premium near NATO waters. For now, the report adds detail and attribution rather than a new event, so the market impact may be limited unless governments act on it.

-

The Leipzig attack was already pinned on Russian military intelligence, but the WSJ’s reporting moves the responsibility up to Putin himself and shows how close Germany came to invoking NATO’s mutual defence clause.

Summary:

  • US intelligence agencies say Putin directly ordered an intensified campaign of sabotage and covert action against NATO countries, according to European officials cited by the Wall Street Journal (gated) 
  • The failed August drone attack on a cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig-Halle Airport was one of the campaign’s opening shots, they said
  • Aides to Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany would have considered invoking NATO’s Article 5 had the attack caused heavy casualties
  • Western intelligence traced the operation to a unit of Russia’s military intelligence, with logistics run through Serbia, where seven suspects have since been arrested
  • A Kremlin back-channel contact warned Berlin after the attack that it would not be the last
  • Russia denies involvement in sabotage in Europe

US intelligence agencies have concluded that Russian President Vladimir Putin personally ordered a stepped-up campaign of sabotage and covert action against NATO countries, with a failed drone attack on a German airport in August among its first operations, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing European officials briefed on the findings.

The attack at Leipzig-Halle Airport, one of Europe’s largest air-cargo hubs, targeted an Antonov freighter used to carry military aid to Ukraine. Germany formally blamed Russia for the attempt in September. The Journal’s reporting goes further, placing the order at the top of the Kremlin and framing Leipzig as part of a deliberate escalation.

Aides to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the newspaper that had the attack caused large numbers of casualties, Berlin would have considered invoking Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, the collective-defence clause that obliges allies to come to a member’s aid. It has been invoked only once, after the September 11 attacks in 2001.

According to investigators cited by the Journal, at least three drones loaded with Semtex were hidden near the airport perimeter and controlled remotely through German mobile networks. One struck the freighter without exploding. German cyber officials traced the communications to servers previously used by Russia’s military intelligence agency.

Western officials attributed the campaign to a GRU branch known as the Special Tasks Service, formed in 2023, and traced the Leipzig plot to one of its department chiefs, already under EU and UK sanctions. Investigators believe a former Russian officer coordinated the ground logistics with Belarusian operatives, using Serbia as a hub to move drones and explosives. Serbian prosecutors have since arrested seven suspects.

The report said European officials have seen a sharp rise in so-called grey-zone attacks since August, including arson against drone makers in Estonia and Poland, sabotage of Starlink stations in Poland, Lithuania and Bulgaria, and drone strikes on merchant ships in the Black Sea. After the Leipzig attempt, a Kremlin back-channel contact reportedly warned Berlin that more attacks would follow.

Russia has denied involvement, with Putin questioning in September where the evidence was. The Kremlin did not respond to the Journal’s request for comment.

The findings come as Washington pursues a delicate relationship with Moscow, including a diesel supply arrangement and a pause in new sanctions that President Donald Trump has said is aimed at keeping Russia out of the war with Iran. How European governments respond, and whether Washington adjusts its approach, will be the next test. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
